newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Bangui ignores opposition protest call.
newsitem.headline: Bangui ignores opposition protest call.

text.p: A call by the Central African Republic opposition for a stay-home protest over the killing of three dissafected soldiers was largely ignored in the capital Bangui on Tuesday, witnesses said.
The government said it had started an inquiry, which the opposition had demanded, into the deaths of the soldiers, who had taken part in army mutinees which erupted three times over roughly a year.
On Monday, opposition parties suspended their role in the government and called for a stay-home protest against the killings as well as a government inquiry.
But shops and businesses opened normally across the riverside capital on Tuesday and there was no sign of reduced traffic on the streets.
"An inquiry has been opened to determine the circumstances of the deaths of the three ex-rebels," government spokesman Laurent Gomina-Tampali told national radio on Monday night.
Independent sources said the three soldiers were disarmed before they were killed by the paramilitary police on Friday night.
Gomina-Tampali said the national police would be joined in the inquiry by members of an African peacekeeping force and a civilian committee monitoring accords signed to end the mutinies.
The first revolts, in April and May 1996, began as protests over pay but became a movement to overthrow President Ange-Felix Patasse.
The third, which began on November 15, degenerated into ethnic bloodshed. French troops, in the country under a defence pact, restored order and handed over to African peacekeepers.
The mutineers are principally from the southern Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba. Patasse is a civilian from the north, and was elected in 1993.
